title: The dancer takes her bow
hookLine: the ankle bells go quiet and the dancer leaves the stage: Samkhya's picture of the world's show
carry: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance
tomorrow: If no one is bound, who gets free?

cards: The last rhythm of a classical dance recital. The drummer's hands slow. The dancer strikes her final pose, ankle bells ringing, then still.
For a moment nobody in the hall moves. Then she bows, and walks off the stage. She doesn't come back out to do it all again for the same people.
The dance was for them, it was seen, and it's finished. The Samkhya Karika reaches for exactly this scene near its end, when it tries to say what happens once the world has done what it came to do.

teach.b: The verse goes like this, in paraphrase. As a dancer stops dancing once she has shown herself to the audience, so prakriti stops, once she has shown herself to purusha. Hold yesterday's travelers in mind.

Prakriti carried the seer through the forest so that purusha could see. The whole unfolding, everything in the count, has been a performance with one audience in view. The Karika adds two more touches.
First, prakriti is generous. She serves purusha in many ways, the text says, and asks nothing back. Purusha does nothing in return; it can't.
Second, prakriti is modest. The Karika says nothing is more modest than she is. Once she knows she has been truly seen, she doesn't show herself to that seer again.
And a few verses later the text gives the last exchange, almost like a play. One says, I have seen her, and loses interest.

teach.h: I HAVE SEEN HER. I HAVE BEEN SEEN.
teach.b: The other says, I have been seen, and stops. That's Samkhya's picture of freedom: liberation by seeing clearly. Later Samkhya and Yoga call that seeing viveka, discernment.

And notice what it isn't. It isn't fighting the world, or escaping it, or hating it. It's seeing it so completely that its hold just ends, the way a song you've finally understood stops replaying in your head.
The dance isn't wasted. Tomorrow, on the last day of Samkhya: what the seer is left with.

how: The dancer image from the Samkhya Karika is taught in Samkhya and Yoga study as a picture of liberation through discernment.

o: a song recited before the curtain rises
a guide to the steps of classical temple dance
verses that end with a dancer's bow once she's seen

p: once truly seen, doesn't appear again

s: in Samkhya, freedom means fighting the world until you escape it
the Karika's picture is seeing: once prakriti is truly seen, her dance ends.
she serves purusha in many ways and asks nothing back.
purusha repays prakriti for the dance
purusha does nothing in return. it only watches.

games.q: you're the dancer. the last pose is held, and you know the audience has truly seen the whole dance. what now?
o: an encore, the same dance again.
bow, and walk off the stage.
games.why: the Karika says prakriti, like a dancer who has shown herself, stops. once she knows she's been seen, she doesn't appear to that seer again.

practice: Pick one sound, a breath, a hum in the room, a car going by, and stay with it from its first edge to its last, letting it finish completely.
Then wait, quiet, until something else steps onto the stage, and watch that one to its end too. If you pray, you can offer each ending as it comes.

wordCard.voice: The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of freedom: prakriti as a dancer who, once truly seen, finishes her dance and leaves the stage.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a dancer; the Samkhya Karika's picture for prakriti, who stops once she has been seen.

carryVoice: Your line: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance. The dancer takes her bow. Until tomorrow.
